DIAPHRAGM WALLS

Temporary or Permanent? Define the Diaphragm Wall’s Role Early

Avoid commercial ambiguity where construction support meets the finished basement.

In this insight

Two roles can carry different expectationsClarify the finished conditionCoordinate acceptance evidencePlan for changes in useFor your project discussionDiscuss a project ↗

Educational overview · Project-specific design and execution require qualified review.

Two roles can carry different expectations

A wall used to enable excavation and a wall intended to form part of the completed structure may require different coordination and acceptance discussions. Some projects combine roles, but that should be a deliberate design decision. A client should ask which responsibilities belong to the temporary works team and which belong to the permanent works designer. Do not let a single drawing title obscure that distinction.

Clarify the finished condition

Discuss the expected final interface with internal walls, waterproofing, slabs and architectural finishes. The contract should identify what the wall contractor is required to deliver and what subsequent packages will add. Terms such as finished wall can mean different things to different teams. Written performance requirements and interface details are more useful than a general expectation of a completed basement.

Coordinate acceptance evidence

Ask the responsible designers to specify the documents and reviews needed for each intended role. Procurement should then ensure that the work package includes those deliverables. Where another contractor depends on the wall’s geometry or embedded details, agree when relevant information will become available. Late discovery of a documentation gap can delay the next package even when physical work appears complete.

Plan for changes in use

If the project changes its basement layout or structural concept, revisit the wall brief rather than assuming the original agreement still applies. Document the technical and commercial consequences together. Keeping temporary and permanent obligations visible makes it easier to assess such changes, allocate design responsibility and avoid an informal transfer of risk to a party that did not price or design for it.

For your project discussion

Use these questions to structure a conversation with the project’s qualified design and delivery team. This article is general procurement guidance, not a site-specific design, method statement or compliance assessment. The cited international resources provide background; applicable local requirements and the approved project documents govern the work.

Take this into your next conversation

  • Separate temporary and permanent responsibilities.
  • Define the required finished interfaces.
  • Revisit the brief when the structural concept changes.
